title: Wendell and the Drop
premise: Silas Galloway, a freelance interpreter who cleans up the linguistic wreckage of doomed peace negotiations, receives calls on a burner phone that shouldn't exist — the voice on the line is their own. The caller claims to be Silas from three days in the future, warning that a courier known as 'the Drop' will hand them a secret worth killing for at the Verrazan border checkpoint. As assassins from two delegations converge, Silas discovers the voice is not future-Silas but a twin sibling erased from their past, using the ruse to smuggle out evidence of a massacre both governments buried. To survive the checkpoint shift change, Silas must publicly trade away the secret — their own true identity and name — choosing found family over bloodline, and letting the world believe they were never Silas Galloway at all.
about_author: Sable Thornbury is the pen name of a former conference interpreter who spent a decade working backroom negotiations across three continents before turning to fiction. They write thrillers about people whose job is to be invisible, drawing on the border towns and half-finished peace accords they can never fully talk about.

chapters.title: The Interpreter's Silence
chapters.summary: POV Silas. At a collapsing ceasefire talks in Grayhollow, Silas renders a general's threat into diplomatic nothing and watches the delegation fail on schedule. Establishes their craft: being trusted by everyone, belonging to no one. Emotional beat: competent loneliness — Silas is fluent in nine languages and homeless in all of them.

chapters.title: A Phone That Shouldn't Ring
chapters.summary: POV Silas. In a rented room, an unregistered burner in Silas's own coat pocket rings. The voice is theirs — identical down to the old jaw injury. The caller says: 'In four days you'll meet the Drop. Don't take the package.' Silas assumes a con, but the voice knows things only Silas knows. Beat: unease curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: Delegation of Ghosts
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Silas re-joins the peace delegation as it travels toward the Verrazan border, cataloguing the players: weary mediator Odile Ferrant, hawkish aide Bram Kessler, and a young courier nobody assigned. Silas tests the phone's predictions; two come true within hours. Beat: the vertigo of trusting a stranger wearing your voice.

chapters.title: What the Voice Knows
chapters.summary: POV Silas. On a night train, the caller describes Silas's childhood in impossible detail — a house, a fire, a second bed. Silas lies awake dismantling the memory for fraud and finds none. Flashback seeds: the orphanage records that end abruptly. Beat: grief surfacing under suspicion.

chapters.title: The Courier Called Drop
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Silas identifies the unassigned courier: a quiet woman called Nell who moves like someone trained to be forgotten. When Silas corners her, she denies everything — in a dialect spoken only in the district where Silas was born. Beat: recognition without proof; the first crack in Silas's cover story to themselves.

chapters.title: Men Who Don't Sign In
chapters.summary: POV alternating Silas/Nell. Two men arrive at the delegation's hotel claiming to be auditors; Nell clocks them as cleaners. She warns Silas obliquely, testing whether he's hunter or prey. Silas realizes the 'future' warnings are really surveillance reports. Beat: alliance forming between two liars.

chapters.title: Kessler's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Aide Bram Kessler privately offers Silas triple pay to mistranslate one clause — proof the delegation is theater and someone expects a package to move through it. Silas declines and immediately regrets the honesty. Beat: the cost of integrity priced in danger.

chapters.title: Three Days Out
chapters.summary: POV Silas. The voice gives coordinates: the Drop happens at the border checkpoint during shift change, when cameras blink. It also says: 'You'll want to save me. You can't.' Silas runs the checkpoints' rotation schedules obsessively. Beat: dread becoming methodical preparation.

chapters.title: Nell's Dialect
chapters.summary: POV Nell. In her only POV chapter, Nell reviews microfilm of a village burned in the Marrow Valley — the massacre both governments deny. She memorizes faces, including two children pulled out alive. One child's file photo is Silas. Beat: cold purpose hiding a sister's terror.

chapters.title: The Fire Nobody Reported
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Silas digs into their own adoption records and finds the Marrow Valley fire — same date as the voice's memories. A second child's name is redacted everywhere. Silas begins to suspect the caller isn't from the future but from the past. Beat: identity cracking open like ice.

chapters.title: Ambush at the Weighbridge
chapters.summary: POV Silas. The cleaners move early, off-schedule, forcing the Drop ahead of plan. Nell passes Silas a sealed envelope mid-chaos and takes a bullet graze covering the escape. The voice screams in Silas's ear: 'Not like this — shift change, not now.' Beat: adrenaline, guilt, the plan broken open.

chapters.title: What Was Worth Killing For
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Silas opens the envelope: photographs, radio logs, and a signed order for the Marrow Valley operation — bearing Kessler's countersignature. The secret isn't just a massacre; it's ongoing, the valley resettled for a mining concession. Beat: moral horror replacing personal mystery.

chapters.title: Odile's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Silas brings partial truth to mediator Odile Ferrant, offering the evidence if she forces it into the record. Odile, career-cautious, hesitates — she's seen whistleblowers buried with their documents. Beat: hope negotiating with cynicism, and losing ground.

chapters.title: The Voice Explains
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Cornered by Silas's questions, the caller finally admits: she is Wren, the redacted twin, alive inside the syndicate that owns the Drop network. The 'future' act was the only way to reach a sibling trained to trust no one. Beat: fury, relief, and the raw ache of found family redefined as actual family.

chapters.title: Cleaners Close In
chapters.summary: POV Silas. The syndicate traces the burner; the hotel is compromised. Silas and wounded Nell run through Grayhollow's freight yards while Kessler's men sweep the district. The voice guides them via back channels, burning her own cover with every call. Beat: hunted intimacy — trust forged at sprint pace.

chapters.title: Copies and Leverage
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Hiding in a print shop, they duplicate the evidence three ways: to Odile, to a foreign press contact, and to a dead-drop only Wren can reach. Kessler makes a counteroffer — Silas's life and a new identity abroad for the originals. Beat: temptation laid out cleanly, almost reasonably.

chapters.title: Shift Change
chapters.summary: POV Silas. The checkpoint rotation shifts at dawn; cameras blink for ninety seconds. That window is the syndicate's last chance to retrieve the originals and kill everyone who touched them. Silas chooses to stand in the open at the checkpoint, making himself the loudest possible target. Beat: deliberate sacrifice as strategy.

chapters.title: Ninety Seconds
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Climax. Amid the shift-change chaos, Wren arrives in person — first time face to face. Kessler's cleaners close; Nell holds the line bleeding; Odile, moved at last, broadcasts the evidence over the delegation's open channel as the window closes. Kessler falls; the syndicate's local network unravels in the glare. Beat: everything staked, everything spent.

chapters.title: The Trade
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Aftermath turns on the blurb's trade: to shield Wren from extradition and bury the syndicate's retaliation, Silas surrenders the one secret worth killing for — his legal identity — signing papers that dissolve 'Silas Galloway' into a protected witness shell. Beat: liberation disguised as loss.

chapters.title: Names We Choose
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Stateless for seventy-two hours, Silas experiences a strange lightness — no delegation, no cover story, no performance. Nell, recovering, offers him a place in the small network of couriers and translators who protect each other. Beat: belonging offered without conditions.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: POV Silas. Silas and Wren sit across a table in a safehouse and compare the same childhood from opposite sides of the fire — what each remembers, what each invented to survive. They agree not to force kinship, just proximity. Beat: reconciliation as slow work, honestly rendered.

chapters.title: The Next Delegation
chapters.summary: POV Silas. A new failed negotiation summons an interpreter with no verifiable name; Silas takes the job under a chosen one, Wren's number saved under no label at all. The burner rings once — this time it's just his sister checking in. Beat: resolution — identity rebuilt from choice, family answered on the first ring.
